feed.title: [BIP Draft] Segregated Data: a prunable, script-isolated block region for data carriage

entry.title: [BIP Draft] Segregated Data: a prunable, script-isolated block region for data carriage
entry.summary:
The discussion revolves around the efficacy of a proposed Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) that seeks to address the issue of data spamming on blockchain nodes. The proposal suggests that instead of all nodes mandatorily storing data, there could be a differentiation in node capabilities—somewhere between Simplified Payment Verification (SPV) nodes and full nodes. This would ostensibly allow users to choose the type of data they wish to store and the level of trust they are comfortable with.
However, there are significant practical challenges to implementing such a change. One major obstacle is user inertia; many users may not readily abandon using SPV nodes for a new system, despite potential benefits. Furthermore, the effectiveness of this BIP is under scrutiny because it does not alter the fundamental incentives for users to change their behavior. Users typically do not bear the direct cost of storing data on-chain, leading to no real incentive to limit what is stored.
Moreover, the suggestion to isolate spammers into a separate area is noted as theoretically sound but impractical in execution. For a substantial shift in user behavior, individuals would need to experience direct consequences from data loss, such as losing coins, which diverges significantly from the current security model reliant on peer-to-peer support. Achieving consensus on such a radical change seems unlikely without massive data accumulation over extended periods.
In conclusion, while the technical framework of the proposed BIP might function under ideal conditions, the lack of practical incentives and the difficulty in altering entrenched user behaviors and systemic structures mean it is unlikely to be adopted or effective in the real world. This reflects a broader issue within technological governance, where theoretical solutions face hurdles in practical application due to existing user habits and systemic inertia.
